items.text:
Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
November 21, 2026
A US-French man has been convicted on federal arson charges connected with the 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles, California, which killed 12 people and devastated the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
The weeks-long blaze destroyed some 6,800 homes and other structures, causing estimated property losses of $150 billion (€136.7 billion).
What was the man convicted of in the Palisades fire case?
A US District Court jury in Los Angeles found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025.
While the fire was initially suppressed, it continued smoldering underground and reignited days later amid fierce winds to become the highly destructive Palisades Fire.
The man is set to be sentenced on March 17. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that he could face up to 40 years in prison.
The man was arrested in October 2025, and already faced one trial five months ago that ended with a hung jury. The judge declared a mistrial in June, prompting federal prosecutors to retry the case under modified charges.
Prosecutors said security camera footage and location data from the defendant's cellphone showed he was the only person nearby when the January 1 blaze began in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
At both trials, they characterized the man, a former Uber driver, as a loner who held a deep resentment against society, and particularly the wealthy.
The defense argued that the initial blaze could have been caused by fireworks, while prosecutors said there was no evidence that any had been set off in the area.
In March, the man denied in a court declaration that he had willfully started any fire, though he declined to testify in his own defense at either trial.
Double fire disaster
The Palisades blaze erupted almost at the same time as another wildfire that broke out in Eaton Canyon, some 30 miles (48 km) to the east.
That fire, believed to have been ignited by sparks from an electrical transmission tower, killed 19 people and devastated the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.
Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster ever seen in Los Angeles County.

items.text:
US Agriculture Department and FBI hit by cyberattacks, media report
Hackers breached systerms at the US Agriculture Department and the FBI, US media reported, amid a recent wave of major technology disruptions across the country.
The US Agriculture Department and the FBI were breached by hackers in cyberattacks, US media reported on Friday, as concerns deepened over the recent spate of tech outages at key American institutions.
The incidents were first reported by NBC News and CNN respectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.
Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the United States, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.
Read more'Is this a cyberattack?' Grounded flights, a Microsoft outage and AI chaos fuel cybersecurity fears
US President Donald Trump has sought to calm the public and urged people to "relax", while officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyberattack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials.
The hackers may use the payments system as a backdoor to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.
The USDA deals with "a bunch of scary biologic issues" and "if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information... they could use our own research against us," a former official was quoted as saying.
CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.
The federal agency was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.
The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.
Read moreWhite House fires national cyber director over widespread outages
"Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety," a former FBI official told CNN.
The former official expressed concerns that hackers "could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on."
AFP has contacted the FBI and USDA for comment.
The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages like the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration.
In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.
The White House fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross this week as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: UDA, ODM, DCP among 94 Parties that fail IEBC nomination rules test as only 11 qualify
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – The United Democratic Alliance (UDA), Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and Linda Mwananchi are among 94 political parties that have failed to meet the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) requirements for nomination rules ahead of the 2027 General Election.
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – The United Democratic Alliance (UDA), Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and Linda Mwananchi are among 94 political parties that have failed to meet the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) requirements for nomination rules ahead of the 2027 General Election.
The three parties were listed among those whose nomination rules require amendments following the commission’s first review of submissions made by political parties seeking to participate in next year’s elections.
Only 11 political parties were found compliant with the applicable legal requirements, raising questions about the preparedness of political outfits for the nomination process ahead of the August 10, 2027 General Election.
The 11 parties that passed the first review include Kenya Moja Movement Party, Wiper Patriotic Front, Jubilee Party, Safina Party, The Mwananchi Party, Liberal Democratic Party, Grand Dream Development Party, Democratic National Alliance Party, Chama ya Mapatano of Kenya, Vision for Development Alliance and Forward Kenya Party.
Other prominent parties that failed to meet the requirements include Azimio la Umoja One Kenya Coalition Party, Maendeleo Chap Chap, Kenya African National Union (KANU), Democratic Party of Kenya, Democratic Action Party-Kenya and Third Way Alliance Kenya.
In a statement issued on Thursday, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon said the commission had communicated the findings to the affected parties and identified specific areas requiring amendments.
“The Commission has completed the first review of the nomination rules submitted by political parties intending to participate in the 2027 General Election,” Ethekon said.
The review was conducted in accordance with Article 88(4)(d) of the Constitution and Section 27 of the Elections Act, which mandate the commission to examine political parties’ nomination rules to ensure compliance with electoral laws and regulations.
The commission assessed several aspects of the rules, including the structure and mandate of party election boards, procedures for identifying and nominating candidates, eligibility requirements for aspirants and the conduct of party primaries.
It also examined provisions governing party lists, internal dispute resolution mechanisms, compliance with electoral laws and measures to address electoral malpractices.
IEBC said the parties found non-compliant had been given details of the deficiencies and were required to amend and resubmit their nomination rules within the applicable timelines.
However, the commission clarified that failing the first review did not automatically disqualify a party from participating in the 2027 General Election.
“The statutory framework provides for the review of nomination rules and, where deficiencies are identified, requires the Commission to communicate the areas requiring amendment,” the statement said.
The commission said the process was intended to give political parties an opportunity to align their rules with the law while safeguarding the integrity of the nomination process.
It further emphasised that party nomination rules must provide for transparent, fair, inclusive and lawful processes, including meaningful participation of women, youth, persons with disabilities and other special interest groups.
The review marks an early milestone in preparations for the 2027 polls, with IEBC urging political parties to address the identified shortcomings promptly ahead of the commencement of nomination activities.
The commission said it would continue engaging political parties and other stakeholders to ensure credible, transparent, inclusive and peaceful nominations.

Today on Sky Sports Racing: Ascot, Lingfield Park and Newcastle feature live on Saturday
In Saturday's feature race, Blow Your Wad will attempt to gain revenge over old rival Doyen Quest in the 1965 Chase at Ascot; we also have competitive action from Lingfield Park and Newcastle live on Sky Sports Racing from 11am
Friday 20 November 2026 13:28, UK
We have a busy day's racing on Saturday with action from Ascot, Lingfield Park and Newcastle, live on Sky Sports Racing...
12.55 Ascot - Doyen Quest and Blow Your Wad clash
Doyen Quest and Blow Your Wad headline a classy field for the Ladbrokes 1965 Chase at Ascot.
Dan Skelton's Doyen Quest outpointed Blow Your Wad when claiming the Grade Two Oaksey Chase at Sandown on his final start last season but could only manage third of three on his return at Carlisle. With that run behind him he ought to be sharper here.
Blow Your Wad should handle this quicker ground and, having progressed through the grades last season, warrants respect as he receives weight under Freddie Mitchell.
- Nicholls breaks record for Jumps wins with Warwick triumph
- Sober Glory storms to victory over Old Park Star on chase debut
Sam Thomas fields Steel Ally who is three from four over fences with his sole defeat coming in the Arkle at Cheltenham in March. He goes well fresh and looks to have the most scope to improve.
Master Chewy completes the quartet.
1.30 Ascot - Classy hurdlers Lucky Place and Kateira head field
Classy hurdlers Lucky Place and Kateira clash in a trappy edition of the Grade Two Ladbrokes Ascot Hurdle.
Lucky Place took this race in 2024 and, having tried fencing, he reverted to hurdles with a few solid runs including when runner-up in the Grade Two Select Hurdle at Sandown. Third behind Alexei in the Molyneux at Aintree on his reappearance, this extra distance should be more to his liking.
The Dan Skelton-trained Kateira looks the obvious danger. She has a bit to find on the figures but produced an excellent effort to beat off La Conquiere at Wetherby and deserves a crack at this valuable prize.
Harry Fry's Altobelli was last seen finishing runner-up behind Potters Charm at Windsor in January and would have claims on the pick of his form.

2.05 Ascot - Decent mares handicap hurdle - That's Nice will be popular.
2.40 Ascot - Berkshire National - Last year's winner Rock My Way takes on Our Power.
3.18 Ascot - Vanderpoel bids to follow up his recent course success.
11.30 Lingfield - Excellent Class Three novice - Wootton Bassett gelding El Mutamaken features. Al Lazzaz is a well-bred type for the Richard Hannon team.
12.00 Lingfield - Fair novice with Bibury Star looking to go one better.

items.text:
Three El Salvador soldiers die in explosives accident in Haiti
November 21, 2026
Three Salvadoran soldiers were killed in Haiti while handling explosives, El Salvador's military said on Friday.
The incident marks the first officially reported deaths since a 2,000-member Salvadoran military contingent was deployed to the gang violence-stricken Caribbean nation last month.
One of the soldiers succumbed to his injuries while being treated in the neighboring Dominican Republic, where he was airlifted to, the El Salvador military said on X.
Another soldier was wounded in the incident and is out of danger, it added.
It was not immediately clear where the blast took place.
The Salvadoran military's statement also did not give any further details on the type of explosives the soldiers were working with.
"We extend our deepest condolences and solidarity to the families of the three deceased," it said.
Why are El Salvador's troops deployed in Haiti?
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele sent over 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti to rescue four El Salvador airmen — members of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF)— who went missing after a gang ambush on October 18 in the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince.
The additional troops dispatched by Bukele are not part of the GSF, and the contingent's remit appears to have broadened to stamp out Haitian gangs.
Bukele, who has been known for his tough approach to the gangs in El Salvador, has posted several videos of strikes on residences of gang leaders around Port-au-Prince.
Haiti announces deal with El Salvador to build new prisons
Meanwhile, on Friday, Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador to build three new Haitian prisons.
The development follows this week's visit to El Salvador by Haiti's security and justice minister, Patrick Pelissier.
The prisons will be built by a Salvadoran company in collaboration with a Haitian firm, Pelissier said.
Haitian prisons are notoriously overcrowded. In 2024, gang raids in two of the country's biggest penitentiaries saw thousands of inmates being released.
El Salvador, on the other hand, is home to a notorious maximum security mega-prison known as Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT).
The country has imprisoned over 90,000 people with no access to family visits ever since entering a state of exception in 2022.
Pelissier visited CECOT during his trip to El Salvador.
"Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again," the Haitian minister said as he praised the mega-prison.

Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
Pressure from within Sudan may achieve what international diplomacy has not.
It has been more than three years since war erupted in Sudan, and its consequences continue to worsen. More people continue to be displaced and require basic humanitarian assis
items.text:
Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
Pressure from within Sudan may achieve what international diplomacy has not.
It has been more than three years since war erupted in Sudan, and its consequences continue to worsen. More people continue to be displaced and require basic humanitarian assistance to survive. On the surface, the conflict appears set to continue indefinitely.
At a recent Security Council briefing, a United Nations official noted: “The picture is bleak. … The parties continue to show no credible commitment to compromise or to pursuing a negotiated pause in fighting. They are not moving closer to dialogue.”
This assessment reflects the international consensus so much so that the United States has chosen in recent months to heap sanction upon sanction in a bid to “raise the costs of continued conflict” for the warring sides and force them into ceasefire talks. But what the view from New York and Washington misses and what became obvious after only a few days in Khartoum this month is that the conditions for a ceasefire are rapidly emerging from within the country.
A perfect storm of financial collapse, military advances and humanitarian catastrophe, along with growing civilian demands, is creating the long-elusive pressure for a ceasefire that could well take hold before the fourth anniversary of the war next April.
Khartoum, Sudan’s beleaguered capital, is no longer the ghost town that it was throughout much of the war. International flights now arrive regularly at the city’s modest airport from Cairo, Riyadh and Doha, carrying Sudanese looking to restart the lives the war put on hold and businessmen sensing a ceasefire on the horizon and angling to get in on the ground floor of the country’s rebirth. At one of the city’s leading business hotels, the lobby was buzzing with British, Swiss and Saudi business groups there to close deals on everything from mining to commodity trading to reconstruction.
But Sudan’s leaders don’t just see the opportunities; they are also feeling the pressure of an economy in freefall. The week I was there, the Sudanese pound fell to a then-record low of 9,000 to the US dollar, compared with a pre-war average of 600. (The exchange rate now exceeds 10,000.) Petrol queues stretched for blocks, even for those lucky enough to be able to afford to fill their tanks. Many of Khartoum’s returnees, more than 2 million of the roughly 3.8 million people who fled, are struggling to buy groceries and keep the lights on. Worse still, farmers can no longer afford fertiliser, leaving much of the country’s most productive cropland lying fallow.
A senior official acknowledged to me privately that the war economy, which enabled Sudan’s army to procure the weapons needed to turn the tide of the war, is now the greatest source of pain for the country’s population. The pressure on Sudan’s leaders to reverse the economic decline is real and is creating a new demand to end the fighting.
Friendly states like Turkiye and Saudi Arabia have pitched in, pursuing agreements to secure fuel supplies and rebuild energy infrastructure, but such support remains limited and temporary. Protests over transit costs recently broke out in Atbara, the northern city where protests against skyrocketing bread prices began in December 2018, helping to spark Sudan’s 2019 democratic revolution. Economic protests unified the country before and could do so again, and the military knows it.
Beyond the economy, it is the military’s battlefield gains that are creating the conditions for it to contemplate a ceasefire. Army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has promised to reclaim “every inch” of territory. He has succeeded in pushing back a new offensive in southeastern Sudan’s Blue Nile State and is advancing farther west in West Kordofan, where the army and its allied Joint Forces recently retook the strategic town of el-Khuwei and several surrounding areas, increasing the army’s control to roughly two-thirds of the country.
Fighting for control of the western region of Darfur, the only region almost entirely under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary, could be costly and time-consuming. But a year after the fall of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur State, to the RSF amid atrocities that a UN fact-finding mission said bore the hallmarks of genocide, efforts to retake the area would demonstrate that the military’s commitment to unify the country wasn’t just battlefield bravado. Making inroads in Darfur would also paint the RSF into a corner and give the army both tactical gains and a strategic advantage in ceasefire discussions.
The final reason why a ceasefire has become so urgent is the spiralling humanitarian crisis in the country, which has been at crisis levels for months but could well become catastrophic by year’s end. Adding to the internal displacement, restrictions on humanitarian access and lost food production is this year’s “Super El Nino”, which has disrupted Sudan’s annual rains and devastated whatever meagre harvest was expected.
With more than 40 percent of the population already facing “acute food insecurity”, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification hunger monitor, projections suggested that Sudan’s hunger crisis could deteriorate dramatically by mid-2027 when food shortages are expected to be at their most severe. The only way to avoid or even mitigate that outcome would be through a ceasefire in the coming months that enables a massive influx of lifesaving aid.
As conditions on the ground make a ceasefire more urgent, Sudan’s own plans for the day after the fighting are becoming clearer. With each ceasefire proposal the military rejects, public demand for a deal grows as people become increasingly exhausted by the war.
Talk of an inter-Sudanese dialogue, political reconciliation and eventually elections is also becoming more common, creating greater expectations that fighting should soon come to an end and responsibility for day

items.title: IEBC: Opposition walkout denied Kenyans chance to address electoral concerns
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has challenged opposition leaders who walked out of a consultative meeting over preparations for the 2027 General Election, insisting that abandoning dialogue will not resolve concerns about the credibility of the pol
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has challenged opposition leaders who walked out of a consultative meeting over preparations for the 2027 General Election, insisting that abandoning dialogue will not resolve concerns about the credibility of the polls.
The commission, in a strongly worded statement issued on Friday, accused the leaders of leaving before substantive discussions could begin, saying their departure denied them an opportunity to scrutinise its election preparedness and deprived the country of a chance to hear their proposed reforms.
The Thursday meeting at Iconic Plaza in Nairobi descended into a confrontation after opposition leaders, led by former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, rejected the agenda presented by the electoral agency.
The leaders argued that the programme did not capture fundamental concerns they had repeatedly raised about the management of the August 10, 2027 General Election.
They demanded that the commission first address their proposals on electoral reforms before proceeding with its own presentation on preparations for the polls.
IEBC hits back
In its Friday statement, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon expressed regret over the walkout, saying the commission had adjusted its programme to accommodate requests from opposition leaders, including changing the scheduled starting time.
He said the leaders left after presenting their preliminary remarks and demands, before the commission could make its presentation or begin substantive discussions.
“The Commission, however, regrets that a section of the Opposition leaders opted to leave the meeting after making their preliminary remarks and presenting their demands, before the Commission could make its presentation and substantive dialogue could commence,” the statement read.
Ethekon said the leaders consequently missed an opportunity to receive first-hand information about the commission’s preparedness, achievements, outstanding challenges and measures being implemented ahead of the 2027 polls.
He added that the commission and the Kenyan public were also denied an opportunity to hear the opposition’s proposed minimum demands and electoral reform recommendations.
“Walking away from dialogue before substantive discussions begin does not advance the resolution of electoral concerns. It deprives all parties of the opportunity to exchange views, clarify positions and build consensus on matters that are critical to the credibility of the electoral process,” IEBC said.
The commission maintained that political parties had a legitimate role in proposing reforms and holding electoral institutions accountable but insisted that such concerns should be addressed through structured consultations.
It invited political parties to submit their proposals formally, promising to examine them within its constitutional and legal mandate and engage other institutions where necessary.
IEBC further defended its independence, citing Article 249 of the Constitution, which provides that independent commissions are subject only to the Constitution and the law and cannot be directed or controlled by any person or authority.
It nevertheless acknowledged that its independence did not exempt it from public scrutiny, accountability or constructive engagement.
Addressing the meeting before the walkout, Gachagua accused the commission of failing to respond to previous requests for engagement, saying opposition leaders had been sidelined in discussions about the electoral process.
He recalled that political leaders had met IEBC in January 2026 and agreed to establish technical teams to facilitate discussions on electoral reforms, but subsequent correspondence seeking to operationalise the arrangement had allegedly gone unanswered.
“Since our meeting in January, you have never called us for a meeting; this is the first time. We have looked at the programme and we have many issues given to us by Kenyans and they are not in the agenda,” Gachagua told the meeting.
He argued that proceeding with the commission’s programme without incorporating concerns raised by political parties would make the engagement meaningless.
“We feel like any discussions that do not include those issues would not be meaningful and would not be useful to the country,” he said.
The former Deputy President proposed that IEBC first engage a technical team appointed by the opposition and led by former Chief Justice David Maraga to develop an agenda that captures the outstanding concerns.
The team, which also includes former Attorney General Justin Muturi and ODM’s Caroli Omondi, was tasked with presenting the opposition’s proposals and engaging the commission on changes needed to strengthen the electoral process.
Gachagua maintained that the opposition was not opposed to consultations but wanted discussions anchored on issues affecting the credibility of the next election.
“We have therefore come to ask that we have appointed a team on electoral reforms led by Maraga to engage with you to draw an agenda that includes the issues that Kenyans have said are important to give birth to a free, fair and credible election,” he said.
He subsequently announced the delegation’s decision to withdraw from the meeting, arguing that the commission’s agenda did not reflect the concerns raised by Kenyans.
“As it is, we are sorry, we apologise because we are unable to participate in this meeting because the agenda does not inform real issues by the people of Kenya,” he said.
The opposition leaders then walked out, with supporters chanting “One Term” in an apparent political message directed at President William Ruto’s re-election ambitions.
Among those who left were Gachagua, Kalonzo, Sifuna, Siaya Governor James Orengo, former Chief Justice Maraga, Muturi and other leaders associated with the opposition’s electoral reform initiative.

items.title: Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
items.summary:
Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
His attacks on Arab lawmakers echo the incitement that preceded Rabin’s assassination and risk unleashing new violence.
Politics is not for the faint-hearted, and debate and disagreement are integral to it. A number of politicians believe that the
items.text:
Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
His attacks on Arab lawmakers echo the incitement that preceded Rabin’s assassination and risk unleashing new violence.
Politics is not for the faint-hearted, and debate and disagreement are integral to it. A number of politicians believe that the end justifies the means, but most know when they are approaching the red lines and when to stop.
Not Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s current prime minister. His repulsive response to the success of the Arab parties in last month’s general election unleashed his darkest racist demons.
Some might argue that this is simply another cynical tactic in his efforts to derail his political rivals’ attempts to form a government. Whether this is who he really is or simply a cynical politician at his core, governing through division makes little difference.
He is the prime minister, and his words and behaviour matter. When he legitimises and normalises this kind of language, he releases the racist genie from the bottle. Certain segments of his supporters may interpret it as a licence to resort to actual violence, and history has precedent for it.
Accusing all 19 elected members of the Knesset (MKs) representing predominantly Palestinian citizens of Israel, individually and collectively, of being supporters of terrorism and terrorists, while portraying those members of the Jewish/Zionist parties prepared to form a coalition with them as, for all intents and purposes, collaborators with those who support terrorism against Jews and seek the destruction of the “Jewish state”, amounts to declaring open season on them. In doing so, Netanyahu is abusing the protection afforded to him by his parliamentary immunity, making allegations for which there is not a shred of truth.
If anyone should know better, learn from his past mistakes and express profound remorse for such behaviour, it is Benjamin Netanyahu. No one is more closely associated with the atmosphere of incitement that preceded the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin on November 4, 1995 than Netanyahu.
Rabin became the principal target of the Israeli right’s hatred after signing the Oslo Accords – in other words, for demonstrating the courage to pursue a peaceful end to the conflict between Israelis and Palestinians. The religious-messianic right, including several rabbis, issued a ruling known as din rodef (the law of the pursuer) against Rabin, accusing him of “ceding parts of the Land of Israel to Gentiles”. Yigal Amir, Rabin’s eventual assassin, cited this ruling as justification for his heinous crime. Amir pulled the trigger, but those who orchestrated and fed the campaign of hatred against Rabin bear considerable responsibility too, at the very least morally.
Netanyahu, who was chairman of the Likud party and leader of the opposition at the time, not only failed to condemn this behaviour but notoriously participated in a protest in Jerusalem during which Rabin’s image was portrayed in a Nazi uniform. Rabin’s widow, Leah, later recalled: “There was a Likud rally in Jerusalem not too long ago. They put the figure of Yitzhak, my husband, in the uniform of a Nazi leader and Mr Netanyahu was there. He later talked against it, but he was there, and he didn’t stop it.”
She never forgave him for that. He never apologised or expressed regret.
Several months later, Netanyahu was elected prime minister. Perhaps, in his mind, this electoral victory exonerated him from any responsibility for creating the atmosphere that led to Rabin’s assassination. It may also have reinforced his belief that divisive politics pays off and can take him where he has always felt he belongs: The prime minister’s office.
Now, caught between a sense of entitlement to remain in power that appears stronger than ever and the fear that relinquishing office could jeopardise his efforts to prevent his corruption trial from reaching its conclusion, Netanyahu is allowing racial hatred to pour out of him unabated.
It began during the election campaign, when he foresaw that his chances of forming the next government were slim. It escalated dramatically on election day, when he once again resorted to his vile dog-whistle tactics in a last-ditch attempt to mobilise his supporters. He warned of surging Arab voter turnout and, by that, at least implicitly questioned the legitimacy of their votes compared with the Jewish ones, as they couldn’t bear their success. But that was only the beginning. The day after the election, Netanyahu and his ultra-right-wing partners turned up the volume, raising allegations of irregularities in Arab communities to advance a narrative of a “stolen” election.
Worse was to come. What should have been days of celebrating Israeli democracy, the swearing-in of the new Knesset, became another opportunity for Netanyahu to abuse his parliamentary privilege. Instead of delivering a speech that might have helped unite the nation after a bruising election campaign, he embarked on a jingoistic horror show.
He accused Gadi Eisenkot, whom President Isaac Herzog had tasked with forming a government because he enjoyed the support of a majority of MKs, and his political partners of seeking to establish a government dependent on parties that, according to Netanyahu, “agree that the Jewish state must be destroyed”. He went on to claim that these parties differed only over the kind of Palestinian state they wanted to see emerge from the ruins of the Jewish state: “Whether an Islamic state in the Muslim Brotherhood mould, like Hamas in Gaza, or a nationalist Palestinian state in the Fatah mould. That is the whole difference.”
This amounts to nothing less than portraying Arab political representatives as a fifth column or traitors, while depicting those prepared to form a government with them as collaborators with this supposed ambition, or as dangerously naive for failing to recognise it.

items.title: Jeers, injuries and doubters - White's journey back to the top
items.summary:
Jeers, injuries and doubters - White's journey back to the top
- Published
Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.
A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead
items.text:
Jeers, injuries and doubters - White's journey back to the top
- Published
Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.
A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead in Madrid. They hung on - just - meaning White will always be remembered as the player who scored that winner.
But, for White, the moment represented more than just a goal. It signalled a dramatic turnaround in fortunes for his international career - just four years after many thought his England days were over.
The Arsenal defender has had a tough time on the international stage to say the least.
He left the World Cup in 2022 after a disagreement with then assistant manager Steve Holland and made himself unavailable during the rest of Gareth Southgate's time in charge.
Since returning to England duty in March under Tuchel, the 29-year-old has now established himself as arguably England's best right-back - despite facing jeers from sections of his own fans for his decision to leave that camp.
The defender, who initially arrived at Arsenal from Brighton as a centre-back, has had an excellent start to the season, having played a crucial part in the Gunners' first title win for 22 years last time out.
It hasn't been straightforward for him at Arsenal either though. White has had to navigate his own injury problems and at one point when the defender was struggling for fitness, there was talk that the Gunners should look at moving him on.
But White has battled back and even dealt with competition from Jurrien Timber to remain one of Arsenal's key players.
- People don't know full story behind England exile - White 
  - Published9 November
- 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages 
  - Published5 days ago
White's England journey
"I think just obviously people don't know the full story, because I never said anything and won't put anyone under the bus", White said before the England win over Spain.
The 29-year-old is keen to put the well-covered departure from the World Cup in Qatar behind him.
After his long absence from playing for England, some supporters did not believe that White should return.
His first appearance at Wembley since that incident in a friendly against Uruguay in March was booed by some supporters, loud enough for Tuchel to be asked about it after the match.
That game in itself was dramatic for White, who scored the opening goal for England before giving away the penalty that saw the Three Lions draw 1-1 with Uruguay.
White, who missed the World Cup with injury, had been expecting the reaction from some fans. But he is used to proving himself and changing the perception around him.
Tuchel was keen to back his player and said in the build-up to the Spain game that he hoped that the chapter was closed on White being booed by his own supporters.
"Obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but yes, it's obviously amazing to be here now." White said of his return to England.
White said in that same interview that he would make the same decision again that he did at the World Cup, but it was now time to move on.
His displays show exactly where his mindset is for his country.
He played the final 12 minutes in England's win over Croatia at Wembley before being brought into the starting line-up for England's toughest match of the November international break against Spain.
This new era of England is being dubbed Tuchel 2.0 and White firmly seems to be part of it.
Chelsea defender Reece James is out with injury. He is a big favourite of Tuchel's but cannot be relied upon for every game due to injuries.
White is a key player for the Premier League champions, reliable in defence and a threat in attack while being physically imposing. There is a lot for Tuchel to like.
And with three of his Arsenal team-mates on the pitch as England won the game, and Bukayo Saka to return, White brings the positives of the cohesion of a club side to Tuchel's team.
Arsenal supporters not surprised by his performances
Arsenal supporters will not be surprised by White's excellent performances for England.
Since signing for the Gunners in 2021, not many players can say they have played more of a crucial role in Arsenal's rebirth under Mikel Arteta.
Such is the importance of White, the Gunners attack does not flow as freely when he is not in the side to link up with Martin Odegaard and Saka as he relentlessly produces overlapping runs - a trait he showed when he scored England's third in Madrid.
His team-mates regularly say he is one of the fiercest competitors in training, and he has regularly shown his mentality when it looks as though things are going against him with his club side.
Arsenal signing Timber and a number of injury issues looked to have had White nearing an exit but, such is his determination, each time a challenge comes up he manages to turn it around.
White is a unique character within football, and has even said he doesn't watch the game away from the training ground, but his passion for his profession cannot be doubted.
Gunners fans will know that the level of passion he displayed in Madrid is something he shows every time he is on the pitch for his club side.

items.title: Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?
items.summary:
They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.
But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted
items.text:
They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.
But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.
It was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.
If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.
According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.
They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.
The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?
On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.
“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”
Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.
Most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be said of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.
Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics company founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”
When I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.
When the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.
Later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”
One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.
‘The numbers have to be right’
Before Brighton’s victory over City, I met Mike Cave, the club’s sporting director, at the Lowry hotel in Manchester. A few of the Brighton players wandered around in club tracksuits. Cave wore a suit and tie and his hair was slicked back. He was telling me it was a big day without saying it.
Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear a

items.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
items.summary:
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
- Published
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The
items.text:
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
- Published
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
- What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow 
  - Published14 hours ago
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.
"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

items.title: German President Steinmeier to visit Kenya for talks with Ruto
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21- German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is expected in Kenya next week for a three-day official visit that will focus on strengthening bilateral relations, expanding economic cooperation and deepening diplomatic ties between Nairobi and Berlin.
Steinmeier will be in the count
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21- German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is expected in Kenya next week for a three-day official visit that will focus on strengthening bilateral relations, expanding economic cooperation and deepening diplomatic ties between Nairobi and Berlin.
Steinmeier will be in the country from November 24 to 26, with his programme expected to include high-level discussions with President William Ruto, visits to technology and healthcare initiatives, and engagements with civil society representatives.
According to the National Accreditation Centre, the visit will cover Nairobi and Naivasha, with the German Head of State expected to be received by President Ruto at State House on Wednesday, November 25.
The two leaders are scheduled to hold bilateral talks before addressing the media, followed by a luncheon hosted in honour of the visiting President.
The discussions are expected to provide an opportunity for the two countries to review their longstanding partnership and explore areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, skills development, migration, climate action and security cooperation.
Steinmeier’s itinerary will also include a visit to Tatu City, where he is expected to tour a mobile healthcare initiative operated by Zuri Health, as well as Call Centre International Kenya and CareerBox, organisations associated with the country’s growing digital services and skills development sectors.
The German President is also scheduled to visit Anno’s One Fine Day Art Centre, which promotes arts and creative opportunities for children and young people.
On Thursday, November 26, Steinmeier will travel to Naivasha, where he is expected to visit Crescent Island before holding discussions with representatives of Kenyan civil society. He is scheduled to depart for Germany later in the day.
He will be accompanied by a German business delegation, reflecting Berlin’s interest in expanding commercial partnerships with Kenya and strengthening the presence of German enterprises in the region.
More than 120 German companies operate in Kenya, making the country an important economic partner for Germany in East Africa.
The two countries have cooperation frameworks covering climate change, energy, agriculture, sustainable development, education and vocational training. They also signed a migration and mobility partnership in 2024 aimed at facilitating skilled labour mobility and addressing Germany’s workforce needs.
The visit forms part of Steinmeier’s broader African tour, which will also take him to Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana between November 22 and 26.
It will be his final African tour as German President, having served two five-year terms since assuming office in March 2017. Germany is scheduled to elect his successor in January 2027.

items.title: Van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Sykes in Grand Slam quarters
items.summary:
Michael van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Tom Sykes in Grand Slam of Darts quarter-finals
Michael van Gerwen expected to face Luke Humphries in the quarter-finals but will now take on Tom Sykes and knows he needs to be prepared for a real contest; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts
items.text:
Michael van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Tom Sykes in Grand Slam of Darts quarter-finals
Michael van Gerwen expected to face Luke Humphries in the quarter-finals but will now take on Tom Sykes and knows he needs to be prepared for a real contest; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22
Friday 20 November 2026 18:41, UK
Michael van Gerwen is through to his first premier ranking quarter-final in over a year but he is up against an opponent he probably did not expect.
Van Gerwen put in a stellar display in a battle of two darting juggernauts when he defeated James Wade 10-8 to make it through to the final eight at the Grand Slam of Darts.
The 'Green Machine' battled hard against everything Wade threw at him and, with a late surge and some superb finishing, he got the victory over the line.
Now, he is preparing for a quarter-final in Wolverhampton but instead of the predicted clash with world No 2 Luke Humphries, he is up against the 72nd-ranked player on the Tour in Tom Sykes.
Sykes pulled off a stunning final-leg victory over Humphries to make the quarter-finals on his debut at the major.
The Dutchman was impressed with what he saw from the 'Castleford Tiger' and knows that if he can beat Humphries, then he needs to expect the unexpected.
"Tom did really well against Luke. I didn't expect that, I think no one expected that, because this is the first time he's played such a long format on such a big TV appearance," he said.
"A win is a win and moving forward I think this gives me a lot of confidence.
"I have to face Tom who had a fantastic game against Luke, 100 average, loads of 180s, so I need to make sure I am prepared for anything.
"He is a fantastic player; he's been doing really well lately on the Tour, but now he has to deal with the fact that he's going to be first to 16. He's never been in this situation, so it will be new for him as well.
"But don't get me wrong, if you can beat Luke, he can beat anyone, so I need to make sure I prepare myself for the worst."
Van Gerwen has had well-documented ups and downs in his darting career over the last two years but has had glimpses of the levels everyone knows he can reach, his massive win against Wade the latest.
He admitted that the victory, and the manner of it, helped him overcome some demons about his own game and he is now looking to turn that into consistency.
"Yes, I did (overcome some demons). Of course, when you're not doing what you are capable of, it can be a really frustrating game," Van Gerwen added.
"But then to finally do it and also in the way how I did it, I think that gives me energy also towards the next game.
"I always believe in my own ability, otherwise I wouldn't be here. If I think I can't believe in myself anymore, that's the day I have to stop playing darts.
"But that day is not there, and it won't be there in the next few years, it is as simple as that.
"My consistency is starting to get better, my belief in my own ability starts to get better, if you also look towards the Pro Tours and everything, my game starts to get somewhere, and that's what you want, that's where you put the work in and the effort.
"That is how darts is, and darts can be a really cruel game, but at the moment I am still in so that's a good thing."

items.title: Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
items.summary:
Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
Eisenkot’s fragile alliance must overcome deep ideological divisions to turn its opposition into a government.
As negotiations over the formation of Israel’s next government approach their first deadline of December 6, caretaker Prime Minis
items.text:
Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
Eisenkot’s fragile alliance must overcome deep ideological divisions to turn its opposition into a government.
As negotiations over the formation of Israel’s next government approach their first deadline of December 6, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be seeking to exploit divisions within the opposition ‘change’ alliance trying to oust him.
On Wednesday, he held an undeclared meeting with one of its leading figures, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, in a move that has prompted accusations that Netanyahu is attempting to fracture the bloc from within.
The meeting, which lasted two and a half hours, was described by Netanyahu’s office as a “security briefing”. Sources within the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, however, characterised it as a “strategic disaster”, according to Israeli media.
Bennett had not informed Eisenkot of the meeting in advance, sources told the outlet Ynet. During a subsequent gathering of opposition leaders, Bennett is reported to have argued that they should try to pursue the possibility of a unity government with Netanyahu, Channel 12 reported.
Bennett, a right-winger, is among several prominent figures in the opposition alliance who have previously served in Netanyahu-led governments. Eisenkot himself joined Netanyahu’s emergency unity government following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, serving as a minister without portfolio and a member of the war cabinet.
Avigdor Lieberman, meanwhile – another right-wing member of the opposition bloc – served as Netanyahu’s foreign minister and defence minister.
“Netanyahu is trying to break up the [opposition] bloc for change through Bennett,” a senior figure in the Eisenkot-led alliance told Ynet in an article referencing the numerous pledges by opposition leaders, including Bennett, never to serve within a Netanyahu-led coalition again.
However, given the broad array of ideologies among the coalition leaders, stretching from the hard-right policies of Lieberman to the relatively left-wing platform of Democrats’ leader Yair Golan, and many having previously worked with Netanyahu, it remains unclear how long the bloc can maintain its unity.
Bennett himself was once among Netanyahu’s closest political allies, serving in several of his governments before breaking with him in 2021, when the opportunity arose to form an alternative administration with centrist Yair Lapid. Bennett and Lapid subsequently assembled a cross-party coalition that ended Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office, with Bennett taking the premiership for the first half of its term. But he still shares many policy positions with Netanyahu.
So how cohesive is the opposition coalition, and what could be its potential breaking points?
Here’s what we know:
Is the change bloc united ideologically?
All of the bloc’s members supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – at least at its start – as well as its attacks on several regional states, including Iran and Lebanon.
In terms of domestic policy, however, there are marked differences between members of the alliance.
Both the bloc’s leader, former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, and Bennett’s electoral partner, Yair Lapid, are regarded as relatively centrist figures. By contrast, Bennett and Lieberman are firmly on the right, divided largely by their attitudes towards religion: Bennett is a religious nationalist, while Liberman is a staunchly secular politician with a background in Israel’s Russian-speaking community, increasingly at odds with Israel’s powerful religious political currents.
Standing apart is the left-wing Yair Golan, a supporter of a two-state solution with the Palestinians and an outspoken critic of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which he has accused the government of encouraging or tolerating.
Is the alliance under strain?
Yes.
Beyond the prospect of Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – continually attempting to undermine them, Eisenkot faces the formidable task of finding the additional 13 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. His bloc holds just 48 of the parliament’s 120 seats after the October 27 elections, leaving him dependent on bridging deep political divides among his allies if he is to form a government capable of governing.
Golan has already met political leaders from parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel and spoken enthusiastically about forming a government with their support. However, that suggestion has been rejected by the rest of the bloc, and has provoked fierce opposition, with right-wing protesters even threatening civil war at the prospect.
Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beytenu party holds seven seats, has been particularly emphatic in rejecting any government dependent on Palestinian support. However, his longstanding and highly vocal opposition to the de facto exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service appears to be softening in the face of another possibility: the 13 seats held by the ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism.
Lieberman’s willingness to compromise on conscription risks undermining one of his central electoral promises, as well as those of other opposition leaders, and could prompt a backlash from supporters.
Have the change bloc’s differences come out in the open?
In August, Bennett dismissed Eisenkot’s proposal to allow limited exemptions from military conscription that would cover the ultra-Orthodox as an “insane mistake”, warning that ultra-Orthodox politicians Aryeh Deri and Moshe Gafni would “run circles around” him. Eisenkot subsequently countered, accusing Bennett and Lieberman of engaging in “old politics” and damaging the opposition’s electoral prospects by refusing to agree that the largest party in the alliance should lead the next government.

items.text:
Las Vegas GP: Kimi Antonelli fastest but Max Verstappen on pole from George Russell after dramatic qualifying
Kimi Antonelli was quickest in qualifying but a five-place grid penalty for a new engine means Max Verstappen will be on pole from George Russell for the Las Vegas Grand Prix; watch Sunday's race at 4am (build-up from 2.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event
Saturday 21 November 2026 05:30, UK
Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a five-place grid penalty means Max Verstappen will start on pole position from George Russell.
New Formula 1 world champion Antonelli will start sixth due to a grid penalty for exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation and surprisingly went fastest in a hectic end to Q3.
The Mercedes driver only just crossed the line in time to start a final flying lap and was helped by a huge slipstream from the Racing Bulls throughout the lap to beat Verstappen by 0.258s.

Neither driver was penalised as Verstappen was given a warning for driving erratically when trying to stop Russell from gaining track position in final practice earlier on Saturday.
McLaren's Lando Norris will start third with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar in fourth and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad will start in fifth, his highest career grid position.
Oscar Piastri qualified seventh but the McLaren driver has a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation, so will start 17th, so Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh instead.
Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto had great pace throughout qualifying but were caught up in the traffic chaos in Q3 on the out laps, so only qualified ninth and 10th.
Ferrari had a disaster as they struggled in the cold conditions and on the long straights, so both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were knocked out in Q2
It is the first time no Ferrari driver has reached Q3 since the 2024 Canadian Grand Prix and Hamilton was shocked both he and Leclerc did not get through.

items.summary:

The senator’s arrival on Saturday, November 21, was marked by an ent
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has taken his political mobilisation beyond Kenya’s borders, launching a two-week tour of the United States with a series of planned engagements targeting Kenyans living abroad.
The senator’s arrival on Saturday, November 21, was marked by an enthusiastic reception from members of the Kenyan community, who gathered to welcome him with songs, dance and celebrations.
Travelling alongside Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi and former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, Sifuna is expected to use the visit to strengthen his political networks and sell the agenda of the Linda Mwananchi Movement (LMM), which he leads.
The tour will cover several states, with town hall meetings, community gatherings and political forums forming the centrepiece of his engagements.
New Jersey will host the opening leg of the visit. Sifuna is expected to preside over the inauguration of an LMM office in Hackettstown, marking the movement’s expansion of its political activities beyond Kenya.
The delegation will then head to Pennsylvania, where the senator is scheduled to attend a Sunday service at Grace Community Church in Allentown before meeting members of the diaspora at The Palace Center.
His itinerary also includes stops in Maryland, Washington DC, Texas, Washington State and California.
The overseas outreach comes at a time when political formations are increasingly turning their attention to the 2027 elections, with opposition leaders exploring alliances and positioning themselves for a contest against President William Ruto.
Sifuna, who has declared his interest in the presidency, appears keen to establish a broader support base by engaging Kenyans outside the country, a constituency that has increasingly featured in national political conversations.
In a message to Kenyans ahead of the tour, the senator urged members of the diaspora to attend the scheduled meetings, saying the engagements would provide an opportunity for direct interaction and an exchange of views.
He cautioned that the delegation would not be able to visit every state or city during the two-week programme, but assured those who would miss out that more opportunities for engagement would follow.
The tour is scheduled to end on December 7 with a dinner in Silicon Valley, California.

items.title: 250,000 Kenyans screened for diabetes, hypertension in Boehringer programme
items.summary:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 21 – German pharmaceutical company Boehringer Ingelheim says it has screened more than 250,000 Kenyans for diabetes and hypertension and enrolled over 20,000 patients on treatment since 2022, as it steps up efforts to tackle late diagnosis of non-communicable diseases.
The company,
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 21 – German pharmaceutical company Boehringer Ingelheim says it has screened more than 250,000 Kenyans for diabetes and hypertension and enrolled over 20,000 patients on treatment since 2022, as it steps up efforts to tackle late diagnosis of non-communicable diseases.
The company, through its Access to Healthcare programme, has been taking screening services closer to communities, particularly in rural and underserved areas where access to medical facilities remains a challenge.
George Kuria, Boehringer Ingelheim’s Sustainable Development for Generations and Access to Health Manager for Sub-Saharan Africa, said the initiative was designed to identify patients early and link those diagnosed with the conditions to treatment and continued medical care.
“So far, we have been able to screen more than 250,000 patients since we started, and we have been able to put on treatment more than 20,000 patients in this programme,” Kuria said in an interview with Capital FM.
Implemented in partnership with healthcare providers, including Zuri Health, the programme uses community outreach clinics and screening camps to reach people who might otherwise go without routine medical checks.
Kuria attributed the high number of undiagnosed cases to poor health-seeking habits, the cost of treatment, limited access to medical facilities and inadequate public awareness about non-communicable diseases (NCDs).
He observed that many Kenyans seek medical attention only after developing symptoms or experiencing complications, rather than undergoing routine health checks.
“They seek health services reactively, not proactively,” he said.
Kuria noted that hypertension and diabetes can remain undetected when people fail to undergo regular blood pressure and blood sugar tests, increasing the risk of complications that require more expensive and specialised treatment.
He also highlighted disparities in healthcare access between urban and rural communities, saying major towns generally have better-equipped health facilities, more qualified personnel and greater access to medical information.
In remote areas, however, residents often depend on facilities with limited staffing and resources, while some are forced to travel long distances to receive medical attention.
The situation is compounded by the high cost of transporting medical supplies, inadequate investment in rural health infrastructure and difficulties attracting healthcare professionals to underserved regions.
“Healthcare services must be provided to the community at their doorsteps and not necessarily them moving from where they are to go very far away to access these services,” Kuria said.
He further cited language barriers and cultural beliefs as obstacles to early diagnosis, noting that some communities struggle to understand health information presented in unfamiliar languages or formats.
Others avoid medical examinations for fear of discovering that they have an illness, delaying diagnosis and treatment.
Kuria warned that late detection of chronic illnesses not only increases the cost of healthcare but can also affect patients’ livelihoods, particularly when complications leave them unable to work and dependent on relatives.
He said patients diagnosed at advanced stages often require specialised services, additional medication and referrals to higher-level hospitals, placing a greater financial burden on households and the healthcare system.
The Access to Healthcare programme was launched in 2022 to address some of these challenges, with a focus on improving screening, treatment and long-term management of hypertension and diabetes.
Through its partnership with Zuri Health, the company conducts mobile outreach clinics and community screening camps where residents receive health assessments alongside information on preventing and managing the conditions.
Patients found to have hypertension or diabetes are linked to continuing care, including access to medication through a tiered pricing arrangement and follow-up support.
The programme also incorporates nurse-led health coaching to help patients understand their conditions, adhere to prescribed treatment and maintain regular medical reviews.
Kuria said the follow-up component was particularly important because some patients abandon treatment after diagnosis due to financial constraints, limited access to medication or inadequate understanding of the risks associated with their conditions.
He said the initiative had reached communities across all 47 counties, with particular attention given to rural populations.
“We have visited all the counties in this country, Kenya,” he said.
The intervention comes amid growing efforts by health facilities to expand access to diabetes screening and treatment.
On November 16, Mbagathi County Referral Hospital announced that it had increased the operating days of its diabetes clinic from two to five days a week to improve access to diagnosis, treatment and long-term patient care.
The expansion was aimed at addressing gaps in diabetes management, particularly the need for regular monitoring to prevent complications.
The World Health Organisation estimates that approximately 18 million people died from non-communicable diseases before the age of 70 in 2021, with 82 per cent of these premature deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries.
Kuria called for stronger collaboration between the government and private healthcare providers to expand screening programmes, improve access to medication and increase public awareness of chronic illnesses.
He also proposed introducing education on conditions such as diabetes and hypertension into school curricula to help young people understand risk factors and the importance of adopting healthier lifestyles.
He emphasised that screening alone would not address the growing burden of NCDs unless patients diagnosed with the conditions could also access affordable medication and consistent medical support.

items.summary:
Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain, given 'unanimous support' by cricket board amid 'Sandpapergate' fallout
Pat Cummins confirms he will "100 per cent support" forum Cricket Australia has set up following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations; CA chair David Boon rejects notion Cummins' i
items.text:
Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain, given 'unanimous support' by cricket board amid 'Sandpapergate' fallout
Pat Cummins confirms he will "100 per cent support" forum Cricket Australia has set up following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations; CA chair David Boon rejects notion Cummins' integrity has been "compromised" amid varying accounts from players of 2018 ball-tampering scandal
Saturday 21 November 2026 05:28, UK
Pat Cummins will remain as Test and ODI captain after being given "unanimous support" by Cricket Australia, with the skipper confirming he will take part in the independent forum launched following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations.
Cummins' position had been under increasing scrutiny since Cameron Bancroft wrote a detail-filled account of the scandal in the West Australian newspaper, backing up Khawaja's claims that every member of the 2018 side was aware of the sandpaper plot.
Bancroft - the player caught on camera trying to alter the condition of the ball in South Africa eight years ago - said he was stirred to break his silence by Cummins' vehement denials of knowledge of the scheme in a press conference last week.
- Pat Cummins faces fresh scrutiny over Sandpapergate claims
- Sandpapergate: News and reaction to ball-tampering scandal
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
After Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met Cummins in Sydney on Friday, a statement released on Saturday read: "In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian Cricket and the welfare of all concerned.
"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."
Cummins prepared for 'difficult conversations' in forum
Cummins, who is set to lead Australia in a four-Test series at home to New Zealand from December 9, with the first match in Bancroft's native Perth, said: "Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility.
"I have and never will take that lightly.
"David (Boon) and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.
"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what's needed.
"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."
Boon: Cummins' integrity has not been compromised
Boon added: "We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.
"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised.
"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn.
"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there.
"We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course."

items.summary:
Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
