A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Pal
items.text:
Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
- Published
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.
"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

items.text:
'He's a killer': Zelensky reacts to Trump calling Putin a friend
- Published
Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky has labelled Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" following their meeting in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
On the sidelines of a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin on Thursday, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations on Friday, days after Ukraine badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it has intercep
items.text:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh
Saudi Arabia issues emergency alerts in Riyadh for the third night in a row, as the Houthis threaten ports and a power station.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it has intercepted three ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels towards Riyadh, after a flurry of emergency alerts in the Saudi capital.
The attack early on Saturday morning came two days after a Houthi strike damaged the Public Investment Fund tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper.
It was the third day in a row that Saudi Arabia issued and quickly lifted alerts for Riyadh.
Hours later, the coalition said that it destroyed another drone fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s south. It did not say which province was targeted.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency had issued eight public emergency alerts during a 24-hour period starting at 7:30am Saudi time (04:30 GMT) on Friday.
Escalation over Hodeidah port
In Yemen, the Saudi-led coalition said earlier on Friday that it carried out a “special operation” against the Houthi-held Red Sea port of Hodeidah, as well as “military targets” in the capital, Sanaa.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said the strikes hit “operational capabilities at Hodeidah port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles”, the AFP news agency reported.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has defended the coalition strikes on Hodeidah port, accusing the Houthis of using its facilities to receive smuggled Iranian weapons and conduct military operations.
The Houthis responded by threatening to attack Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports, warning airlines that Saudi Arabia’s airspace was “unsafe”.
They also threatened Riyadh’s financial centre and a power station in Al-Shuqaiq, in the southwest.
The United Nations said it was following the escalation “with concern”.
It warned that continued fighting could threaten vital supply routes for humanitarian aid in Yemen.

items.text:
Brazil ex-president Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
November 21, 2026
Convicted former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.
Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction."
The DF Star Hospital in Brasília said that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.
Bolsonaro's history of hospitalizations
Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.
"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos said.
Son blames house arrest for Bolsonaro's health issues
Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to 2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.
Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.
Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.
Carlos said that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily."
Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida.

items.summary:
Three French police officers sentenced over racist assault on Black man
Paris criminal court finds racism was an aggravating factor in the 2020 assault of Black music producer Michel Zecler.
A French court has sentenced three police officers to serve time for assaulting a Black music producer in 202
items.text:
Three French police officers sentenced over racist assault on Black man
Paris criminal court finds racism was an aggravating factor in the 2020 assault of Black music producer Michel Zecler.
A French court has sentenced three police officers to serve time for assaulting a Black music producer in 2020, acknowledging the racist motives of the beating in a rare ruling against police brutality.
In the judgement delivered on Friday, the Paris criminal court found the victim, Michel Zecler, 47, consistent in his account and deemed that racism was an aggravating factor in the assault.
An investigation into the incident showed that the officers pushed into the entrance of Zecler’s office and beat him.
The officers attacked Zecler outside his studio in Paris on November 21, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, justifying the assault as being for his failure to wear a mandatory mask and allegedly grabbing one of their weapons.
Zecler’s security cameras recorded the attack, which left him with head trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon.
The court noted that Zecler told a Black police officer who was handcuffing him after the beating that he had been subjected to racial slurs. He repeated the allegation at the police station and again on the way to the hospital, and he also told his loved ones.
The court added that the officers’ falsification of the police report damaged their credibility when they denied using racist insults.
The court sentenced Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, to five years in jail, including three suspended.
Philippe Tondeux, 50, was sentenced to five years, including three-and-a-half suspended.
Pierre Plantier, 37, was sentenced to five years, four of which were suspended, and was to serve the one year with an ankle tag instead of behind bars.
A crowd applauded Zecler as he stepped out of the hearing, according to the AFP news agency.
“Justice has been done. It has restored a man’s dignity and allowed him to begin rebuilding himself,” his lawyer, Serge Money, said.
All three officers apologised to Zecler earlier on Friday, with Plantier in tears, AFP reported.
A systemic issue
French victims and researchers say police violence is systemic, but guilty verdicts in alleged police brutality cases are rare in the country.
In 2024, a judge handed suspended prison sentences to three officers who caused permanent rectal injuries to a Black man, Theo Luhaka, during a stop-and-search in 2017.
Last year, a report by France’s rights chief found that young men “perceived as Arab, black or from North Africa” are four times more likely to be stopped than the rest of the population.

UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy

Daniel Thomas, 37, also known a
items.text:
UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy
November 21, 2026
A British anti-migrant activist has been sentenced to 15 months in prison for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel while a French rescue worker was still on board.
Daniel Thomas, 37, also known as "Danny Tommo," pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month. He was sentenced on Friday at Portsmouth Crown Court in southern England.
The activist, who founded the anti-immigration group Patriot Platform, livestreamed the September 22 incident on social media, where it was watched by a large audience.
What happened during the English Channel incident?
Thomas had followed an inflatable boat carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel on September 22.
After the migrants were transferred to another vessel and taken ashore, Thomas approached the empty dinghy, which a French rescue worker had boarded.
Video footage showed him repeatedly stabbing the boat with a knife. Judge James Newton-Price said he counted eight cuts.
During the livestream, Thomas could be heard saying "this is what needs to happen."
He also shouted "get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat ... take them back, no more of these," according to prosecutor Joel Smith.
Newton-Price accepted that there was "no immediate danger" to the rescue worker. However, he said Thomas' aggressive behavior would have been highly alarming.
What did the judge say about Danny Tommo's actions?
Sentencing Thomas, Newton-Price said his actions amounted to "flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption" of the legitimate activities of British and French authorities in the Channel.
The judge highlighted the work of Britain's Border Force, Coastguard and volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI).
"They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover," he said.
Thomas appeared by videolink from a prison in Winchester, southern England, where he has been held since late September after being denied bail.
He reportedly held his head in his hands when the sentence was announced.
Under current UK sentencing rules, Thomas may serve only a third of his 15-month sentence, including time already spent in custody.
The court also heard that he had five previous convictions, including one for kidnapping in 2016.
Who is Danny Tommo and what is Patriot Platform?
Thomas is a longtime ally of prominent far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.
He has built a large online following and founded Patriot Platform, a group campaigning against migrants arriving in Britain in small boats.
Thomas gained prominence earlier this year by leading confrontational anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth and the southeastern port of Dover.
Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and clashed with police.
The demonstrations have increasingly targeted police officers and rescue workers involved in responding to migrant boats arriving on British shores.
The UK government has condemned the protesters' "intimidating and thuggish behavior."
Thomas is also due to stand trial in London next June over several alleged offenses, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing center in Dover in March.
How many migrants cross the English Channel?
Successive British governments have struggled to stop migrants from making the dangerous journey across the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year.
Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain.
Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration campaigners have continued to demand tougher measures to prevent migrants from reaching the country.

US president calls tech giant to give former CEO ‘a second chance’ and urges him to ‘make a big apology’.
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s found
items.text:
Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang
US president calls tech giant to give former CEO ‘a second chance’ and urges him to ‘make a big apology’.
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs.
“You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”
Trump also described Jensen Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions”.
“I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back, because he created something with Blackwell,” Trump said, referring to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.
Huang resigned on November 12, following media reports of an intimate relationship with an alleged spy for Beijing who may have helped route restricted chips to China. US intelligence officials are said to have previously known about the possible espionage link.
Two more affairs have since been reported. The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China’s defence industry through her family and associates.
Trump also appeared to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had said earlier on Friday that Jensen Huang did not come up in talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
“I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man,'” said Trump of his meeting with the Chinese president.
No way back
In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang offered to return to the company.
However, Nvidia’s board has ruled out his comeback. Board chairperson Harvey Jones said on an earnings call later that day that the directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and do not plan to reinstate him.
The scandal has also drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas told The Wall Street Journal that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke, though he stopped short of calling for the commerce secretary’s resignation.
Trump said he still supported Lutnick.
“I have not lost confidence,” Trump said, calling Lutnick “a different kind of a guy, very good businessman”.
Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, are investigating whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm run by his sons, avoid losses tied to scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to a Chinese company.

items.summary:
Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
The new African agency aims to bring greater transparency to credit ratings.
Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative fi
items.text:
Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
The new African agency aims to bring greater transparency to credit ratings.
Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative first endorsed by African leaders in 2017.
The agency, based in Port Louis, Mauritius, is designed to provide independent assessments of African governments and corporate borrowers, drawing on local data and expertise to complement ratings issued by international agencies. Its first sovereign ratings are expected by the end of March.
Its interim chief executive, Sifiso Falala, says AfCRA is already in discussions with 15 African governments with research planned in countries that include Mauritius, Kenya, Togo, the Seychelles and Burundi.
The case for AfCRA rests partly on the cost of how African economies are perceived by financial markets. A 2023 study by the United Nations Development Programme estimated that subjectivities in sovereign credit ratings cost African countries $74.5bn through excessive interest payments and foregone lending.
African governments have long argued that international rating methodologies do not adequately account for the continent’s economic structures and circumstances.
The major international agencies – Moody’s, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings – have disputed suggestions that their assessments systematically disadvantage African borrowers. At a Chatham House discussion in June, Moody’s Marie Diron argued that the agency’s analysis of four decades of global sovereign default data showed that African countries with a particular rating had broadly the same probability of default as equally rated borrowers elsewhere.
For example, she said, a sovereign with a B rating had an estimated one-year default probability of about 5 percent regardless of whether it was African or from another region.
That is an important counterargument. AfCRA’s challenge will not simply be to produce different ratings but to demonstrate that its assessments are more comprehensive, transparent and predictive of actual credit risk. Its credibility will ultimately depend on the evidence behind its conclusions, including when those conclusions are unfavourable to African borrowers.
Transparency and mutual learning
For Falala, the agency’s priority is to ensure that assessments better reflect the economic realities of African countries.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, he said: “A significant number of African countries carry speculative-grade ratings despite having no history of sovereign default.
“This raises legitimate questions about whether prevailing models adequately capture African economic realities. We believe our analytical framework can contribute to a constructive reassessment of these assumptions, encouraging the entire industry to examine whether the indicators used to determine creditworthiness remain relevant, proportionate and sufficiently predictive of actual default risk.”
Falala said the agency was not seeking more favourable ratings for African borrowers but greater accuracy through engagement with established rating agencies.
“Our objective is not to manufacture better ratings for Africa, but to produce more accurate ratings of Africa in collaboration with established rating agencies. Importantly, we believe that a stronger AfCRA will contribute to a stronger credit rating industry overall,” he said.
That distinction will be central to the agency’s credibility. An institution established partly in response to dissatisfaction with existing ratings must demonstrate that its own assessments are independent of political pressure and the interests of the governments and companies it evaluates.
Falala acknowledged the scepticism surrounding the industry, saying AfCRA has an opportunity to rebuild confidence through transparency and analytical independence. He said the agency was not seeking confrontation with established rating providers but saw considerable scope for collaboration and mutual learning.
More local data and methodologies
Beyond sovereign ratings, AfCRA intends to assess companies, municipalities, banks and local-currency debt. This broader coverage could address gaps in information about borrowers that receive limited attention from international agencies while providing domestic investors with additional assessments of credit risk.
The potential benefits extend beyond the ratings themselves. African pension funds, banks and other institutional investors need reliable information to assess domestic borrowers and allocate capital. More comprehensive coverage, supported by stronger local data, could help reduce information gaps and support the development of domestic capital markets.
However, additional ratings will not automatically translate into cheaper borrowing. Their influence will depend on whether investors consider the assessments credible and useful in making investment decisions.
Abdussalam Muazu, an associate chartered economist at the Institute of Chartered Economists of Nigeria, said limited information about African borrowers has contributed to the uncertainty investors factor into lending decisions.
“African governments and companies often pay more to borrow than their ratings suggest, partly because investors know too little about them and price in the uncertainty.
“The big agencies have few analysts on the ground, and much of Africa’s economy runs through informal trade, mobile money and community finance that is hard to measure from outside. An African agency can bring local knowledge into credit ratings and help build the data that is missing today, which gives investors less reason to charge for guesswork,” he told Al Jazeera.
The argument points to a wider problem: The availability and quality of economic data can shape how creditworthiness is assessed. Informal economic activity, for example, is not always adequately captured in conventional indicato

Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
Copenhagen accuses Moscow of planning assassination with banned local gang; Russia says no evidence for allegation.
Denmark has said it is expelling Russia’s defence attaché after accusing Moscow intelligence of plotting to kill a Ukrainian rapper at a concert near Copenhagen.
“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attaché from Denmark” within seven days, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference on Friday.
Denmark is also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians, he added.
The expulsion ultimatum comes hours after Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said it suspected Russia of planning the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb with help of a Danish gang.
Danish public broadcaster DR named the rapper as Kyivstoner, who has both Ukrainian and US citizenship.
“A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia,” PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told journalists on Friday.
“The case shows, in our assessment, that the Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out an execution in Denmark,” he said.
Thwarted plot
According to PET, three people were stopped in a car near the music venue where the rapper was scheduled to perform on September 25. Police found firearms and knives in the vehicle.
Two people were placed under formal investigation on Friday for attempted murder and for helping a foreign intelligence service operate in Denmark. Police and PET suspect Loyal to Familia, a street gang and criminal network banned since 2021, helped plan the attack.
Police and intelligence services made their announcements as two Danish men appeared in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder, court documents showed.
According to the court documents, the suspects were arrested five minutes before the concert was set to begin and one of them had bought a ticket to the performance. The concert was cancelled.
Exchange of reactions
In response to Friday’s announcement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said, “We are facing a cornered Russia, acting more aggressively and with a greater propensity to take risks.” The strongest response would be to “not waver” and to keep supporting Ukraine, she added.
European Council President Antonio Costa said the alleged assassination attempt was “unacceptable” and “will not go unanswered”. He promised Denmark the European Union’s full backing against what he called Russian hybrid attacks.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would give “an appropriate response”, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen called the expulsion “vengeful” and said Denmark had not presented “any evidence of Russia’s involvement in this mysterious crime”.
Copenhagen has accused Moscow of other hybrid attacks, which are acts short of open war, such as sabotage and disruption. In September 2025, drones shut down Copenhagen airport for hours, in what Denmark called a hybrid attack.
PET said in September that Russia was recruiting Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against Danish defence firms with ties to Ukraine.
Russia has denied involvement in such operations.

items.title: Can Mauricio Pochettino save Man United from Premier League relegation?
items.summary:
Can Mauricio Pochettino save Man United from Premier League relegation?
Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time on Sunday, in a trip to rivals Liverpool.
Manchester United will be led by a third manager in three years when Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of his
items.text:
Can Mauricio Pochettino save Man United from Premier League relegation?
Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time on Sunday, in a trip to rivals Liverpool.
Manchester United will be led by a third manager in three years when Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of his first match since replacing Michael Carrick.
The fact that the Premier League clash is against their fierce rivals Liverpool – the team that, with United, are joint record English top-flight champions – is an added twist to a sordid recent tale for the Manchester club.
When Sir Alex Ferguson retired after lifting a then-record 20th league title in 2013, the Red Devils had climbed to the biggest and richest club in the world.
Now, apart from not being able to claim a Premier League crown since 2013, they are laden with debt – and worse still, they sit inside the relegation zone.
Can Pochettino save Man United from relegation?
The last time United were relegated from the top flight was in the 1973–1974 season. That came only six years after one of the club’s greatest nights – the lifting of the European Cup (now the Champions League), making them the first English club to do so.
Their fall this time around has not come quite as quickly, with their last crowning as European champions in 2008, and they have not been relegated – yet.
Few expect them to be. It would be unthinkable given the changed landscape of the entire footballing world, which has become awash with finances that clearly separate the elite and their resources from the rest.
When Pochettino was introduced to the media for the first time on Friday, the gathered press did not mention the word “relegation” even once.
So the simple answer is: yes, he can save the club from relegation. The longer equation is that the alternative would surely be the greatest shock in the history of a game famed for upsets and underdogs.
What problem does Pochettino need to solve first at United?
Words like identity, fitness, formation, and one that Pochettino awkwardly dropped on Friday, “philosophy”, have dogged every manager at Old Trafford since Ferguson’s departure.
“We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, with our own philosophy and how we like to work,” Pochettino told the gathered reporters.
“We need to improve our players, find a way to perform, but the future and identity of the club is very clear.
“It is an historic club with an amazing years competing and being one of the best in the world.
“It is difficult to find another club that is the size of United. We need to be open-minded to do our best, and the players need to buy the idea that we need to improve.
“The job is to get the rest of the historic club, Manchester United, into a different place to where we are now.”
All of that can wait, because Liverpool are the next opponents, and for United, they do not come any bigger.
The Manchester derby has taken on a new level in recent years – although the tide there may also soon turn, depending on City’s appeal against their charges – but the rivalries against the Reds and Leeds United have the deepest roots for United fans.
A recent defeat to the revived latter still weighs heavily.
Pochettino needs to find a way for the team to start winning, and it needs to come soon. The club’s opening to the season is their worst since 1986, and one win – the worst return in the league – has left United just one point off bottom place.
By the time Pochettino and his United players walk out to the hostility of the Anfield crowd, they could be at the very foot of the table.
Will Pochettino change United’s formation?
The easiest part of the equation for Pochettino is the formation. With the United States national team, which he left to join United, the Argentinian deployed the 4-2-3-1 tactic that even Ferguson had evolved to in his final years.
Pochettino’s Tottenham, the club he made his managerial name with, were always set out in the same way with Harry Kane leading the line.
The United squad – which were moved to an uncomfortable 3-4-3 by Carrick’s predecessor, Ruben Amorim – are built for Pochettino’s style, but the task of melding them together had eluded Carrick and will be the key to their imminent return.
What long-term problems does Pochettino face at United?
The off-field troubles at United are well documented. The club are weighed down by the debts accrued with the Glazer family’s 2005 purchase.
Jim Ratcliffe’s investment three years ago has seen the Englishman and his INEOS group take control of footballing matters, but the annual interest the club pays remains a heavy burden.
The ownership is committed to its plan to rebuild the Old Trafford stadium to increase capacity and, with it, move the club to a more sustainable future.
That means the spending power that once saw United lead the way in transfer signings has diminished to the point where they cannot compete financially with Liverpool, City and Arsenal on the domestic front, let alone Spanish giants Real Madrid and Barcelona on the continent.
This is no easy fix for the manager or their owners, and is undoubtedly the long-term challenge for everyone involved.
What signings will Pochettino and United target in January transfer window?
Although the squad is set up for a 4-2-3-1 formation, they lack strength in depth.
Striker Benjamin Sesko has had an injury-plagued start to his United career since his move two seasons ago, and the Serbian international was far from the finished product when he arrived.
The 23-year-old’s absence this season has left a glaring hole up front, with Cameroon forward Bryan Mbeumo admirably leading the line with great endeavour, but lacking the presence a lone striker requires.
Despite needing a world-class finisher and being well stocked at the back, United have problems at the other end of the pitch, shipping 30 goals in all competitions this season.
Only two teams have conceded more than United’s 19 in the Premier League.

items.text:
BJ Callaghan said he remains fully focused on leading Nashville SC through the Major League Soccer playoffs, amid links to replacing Mauricio Pochettino as United States men's national team head coach.
"For me, it's not about me. We've earned ourselves to get to the playoffs here and my job is to be a leader of this team and one of the leaders in this club," Callaghan told reporters on Friday.
- Pochettino: 'Massive' pressure with USMNT makes me better coach for Man United
- Ex-U.S. coach Arena: Federation doesn't 'have a clue' how to replace Poch
- MLS playoff Round 1 predictions: Who will move on to the conference semifinals?
"My focus is 100% on the players, the staff, the fans and overall this soccer club to make sure what happened in the regular season, we can make it an extension into the playoffs because we have more things to achieve here."
Pochettino departed his role as U.S. coach this week to become Manchester United's new coach. U.S. Soccer announced under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo will lead the team during the December international camp while the search for Pochettino's replacement is underway.
Callaghan previously served as an assistant to then-USMNT coach Gregg Berhalter before taking over interim charge in 2023. He led the group to the Concacaf Nations League title and reached the semifinals of the Gold Cup later that year before Berhalter was re-appointed.
Callaghan joined Nashville in 2024 and turned the team into a trophy-winning side.
Nashville lifted the U.S. Open Cup in 2025, when defeating Austin FC, and earned the 2026 MLS Supporters' Shield. Callaghan also inspired the Eastern Conference team to break the league's record for most points in a single season, with 77 points in 34 games, shattering Inter Miami's previous tally.
Nashville will now face FC Cincinnati in the best-of-three round one playoff series starting on Sunday.
Former Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City coach Pep Guardiola has been the biggest name linked to replacing Pochettino. Before his departure following a Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal win over Haiti on Tuesday, Pochettino encouraged anyone interested to take the job.
"It's the perfect moment to arrive to the [U.S. Soccer] Federation," Pochettino told reporters at a roundtable Monday. "Everything is in the right direction. I think, of course, take [it]. Take it because he's going to find really good people, good players. The player can fit for his style; the National Training Center that wasn't [there] before."

"Hirving Lozano has completed his loan with the Galaxy and returned to his parent club, San Diego FC,
items.text:
LA Galaxy announced the club will not exercise the option to permanently acquire Hirving "Chucky" Lozano after his loan spell, as the forward returns to San Diego FC ahead of the 2027 sprint season.
"Hirving Lozano has completed his loan with the Galaxy and returned to his parent club, San Diego FC," the Galaxy announced in a press release when it made its 2026 roster decisions public.
The Galaxy signed Lozano on loan as a Designated Player in August through December 2026, with a permanent trade option included in the contract. He played 10 matches for the club, recording two goals and one assist, before the Galaxy made the decision to end his time with the club.
Lozano originally signed with San Diego FC in June 2025 while still under contract with PSV Eindhoven, months ahead of the expansion team's MLS debut. He finally joined the club in January, playing 27 matches in their inaugural season before conflict led him to the sidelines.
The Mexican forward was first left off the roster for San Diego FC's first-ever MLS playoff match following a report of a locker room altercation. Head coach Mikey Varas hinted that Lozano could be back with the team soon.
Lozano publicly apologized for his reaction inside the locker room before tensions escalated.
By January 2026, sporting director Tyler Heaps and Varas confirmed Lozano would no longer be taken into consideration.
"Our stance remains the same," sporting director Tyler Heaps told ESPN ahead of the team's 2026 season opener. "Hirving is not and will not be part of our sporting plans heading into this year."
Lozano trained independently for months before eventually signing with the Galaxy in August. It remains unclear what his role with San Diego will be in 2027 following his return from the loan spell.
The Galaxy also announced that veteran defender Maya Yoshida will depart after captaining the club for three and a half seasons. The Japan international made 117 appearances across all competitions and was a cornerstone of the squad that captured the club's sixth MLS Cup title in 2024.

items.title: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
items.summary:
ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
- Published
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's loca
items.text:
ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
- Published
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.
At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.
But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.
The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.
It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.
The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.
In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?
It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.
While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.
While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.
The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

items.text:
US judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion cancer settlement
November 21, 2026
A US judge on Friday approved German chemical giant Bayer's $7.25 billion (€6.60 billion) settlement of lawsuits claiming its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer.
Judge Timothy Boyer in the US state of Missouri ruled that the agreement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate."
The decision could help Bayer end years of costly legal battles over Roundup, which the company acquired when it bought US weedkiller producer Monsanto in 2018.
"The court's final approval is a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation," Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said.
The ruling could still be appealed.
How much money will Roundup cancer patients receive?
The agreement covers tens of thousands of people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, after using Roundup.
It also covers people who may be diagnosed with the disease in the future after previous exposure to the weedkiller.
Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion into a special fund over the next 21 years.
Individual payments are expected to average between $10,000 and $165,000. The amount will depend on factors including the patient's age, the severity of the illness and how long they were exposed to Roundup.
Some lawyers representing cancer patients have criticized the payments as too low.
But the judge rejected their objections, saying that further delays could leave seriously ill patients waiting years for compensation.
Christopher Seeger, a lawyer representing cancer patients, welcomed the decision.
"Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," he said.
Why has it become harder to sue Bayer over Roundup?
The settlement follows a major victory for Bayer at the US Supreme Court in June.
The court ruled that Bayer could not be sued under state laws for failing to put cancer warnings on Roundup packaging.
The judges argued that US federal rules did not require such warnings and that individual states could not impose additional labeling requirements.
The decision made it much harder for cancer patients to win lawsuits against Bayer.
In October, a Missouri jury also ruled in Bayer's favor in a separate Roundup cancer case.
However, some legal battles continue. Around 200 cases are still being fought in federal courts outside the new settlement, according to Bayer.
How much have the Roundup lawsuits cost Bayer?
Monsanto introduced Roundup in 1974. Its main ingredient, glyphosate, became one of the world's most widely used weedkillers.
Farmers use Roundup to kill weeds without damaging crops that have been genetically modified to survive the chemical. It has also been widely used in private gardens and on lawns.
Bayer inherited the legal problems surrounding Roundup when it bought Monsanto for $63 billion in 2018.
Since then, around 200,000 claims have been made against Bayer by people who believe the weedkiller caused their cancer.
The company already agreed to a $10.9 billion settlement in 2020. However, it failed to secure approval for a separate agreement covering future cases.
Some lawsuits have resulted in huge payouts, including a $2.1 billion award to plaintiffs in Georgia.
Bayer has already set aside $16 billion for Roundup-related legal costs. Its shares have fallen by 46% since the Monsanto takeover.
The company has also removed glyphosate from newer versions of Roundup sold to private consumers in the United States.
Does Roundup really cause cancer?
Scientists and regulators disagree about whether glyphosate causes cancer.
In 2015, the World Health Organization's cancer research agency classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" to humans.
However, the US Environmental Protection Agency says glyphosate is unlikely to cause cancer when used as directed.
Bayer has repeatedly denied that Roundup causes cancer, pointing to scientific studies and regulatory approvals.
The debate intensified last year when a major scientific study that had supported Roundup's safety for decades was withdrawn.
The journal that published it cited serious problems, including missing cancer research and previously undisclosed involvement by Monsanto employees.
The withdrawal raised further questions about the influence of chemical companies on scientific research.

items.title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
items.summary:
Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
- Published
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
items.text:
Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
- Published
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.
The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.
"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
Kaplan disagreed.
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.
The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.
Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.
The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.
Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.
He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.
Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.
The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

T
items.text:
Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least four in Nigeria
Police say two children among dead as search continues for more victims.
A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of people to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least four people, according to police.
The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, police spokesperson Musa Mohammed told the Reuters news agency.
He said the dead were two adults and two children.
Police said 24 people were rescued, with 19 treated at a local clinic, and five taken to a hospital in the state capital.
Search teams were still looking for more victims, police said. Police did not say how many people were on board, but some residents told Reuters there were at least 300.
Police said the driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
According to a statement from the Bayelsa State Police Command, the accident occurred at the river junction between the Oweikorogha and Otuan communities, in the state’s Southern Ijaw district.
The boat that capsized was travelling “for a burial ceremony”, the statement also said, adding that police are “coordinating efforts with local divers and other responders”.
Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance or failure to comply with safety regulations.
A similar incident occurred in August, when at least 51 died after a boat sank in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto State, and another in January, when at least 26 people drowned after a boat ferrying people from Jigawa to Yobe State capsized.

In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, Unit
items.text:
Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
- Published
Manchester United borrowed another £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.
In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.
United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed £10m on 16 November.
The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to £240m.
The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to £95m. However, that figure is likely to top £100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.
Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.
Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.
The club also confirmed they had spent £5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".
The filing also revealed they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was £577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.

items.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
items.summary:
In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
- Published
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Ant
items.text:
In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
- Published
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
EU warns COP31 risks turning into a ‘fossil summit’ as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal.
The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that n
items.text:
Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
EU warns COP31 risks turning into a ‘fossil summit’ as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal.
The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that no longer mentions fossil fuels.
The two-week talks in Antalya, Turkiye, were due to end on Friday, when a late closing session approved some technical matters, but not the wider political deal.
“We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet,” COP31 President and Turkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates.
Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference said the meeting lacked ambition to address the worsening climate crisis and was on track to be the “worst COP ever”.
A third draft is expected on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.
The fossil fuel fight
An opening draft from cohost and lead negotiator Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.
Oil producers have also resisted similar language at past talks, including at COP28 in 2023. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for money to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.
The European Union said the draft “risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit”. Panama, which signed a letter with a dozen other countries demanding “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”, threatened to walk away from the talks.
“It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told a news conference.
Other contested points
The draft proposes raising the share of the world’s final energy consumption that comes from electricity to 35 percent by 2035. It does not say the power must come from renewables, and some countries want the target to say “clean”.
Some countries also reject a push to expand carbon capture, a technology that traps emissions from power plants and factories. They say it is costly and unproven, and could let polluters keep burning oil and gas.
“We want to see the references to false solutions removed,” said Vanuatu’s climate minister, Ralph Regenvanu.
Developing countries are angry that rich nations are falling short on climate finance. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings.
Tough backdrop
A UN report last month found the world is set to pass the 1.5-degree-Celsius (2.7F) warming limit set under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
The United States, the largest historical emitter, is absent for a second year after President Donald Trump ended climate cooperation.
The US-Israel war on Iran and higher living costs have also drawn attention away from the talks.
Environmental groups say the summit lacks ambition.
“This has been the worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa.

items.title: Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury
items.summary:
Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.
Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied
items.text:
Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.
Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted with the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, saying afterwards that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.
A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”
The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled things up when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.
The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, with the first leg in Norway taking place on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “currently discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.
Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.
Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Michael Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.
Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.
Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone as Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.
Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by defender Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.
The hosts levelled 17 minutes later as full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return to the field for the second half, and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.
Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig just before the hour mark. Recent Germany call-up El Mala then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.
Now a point behind Bayern, chasers Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first in the table if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.
Kane earlier this month signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029 which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.
Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has bagged an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

items.summary:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of
items.text:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.
But tech stocks more broadly also fell.
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

items.summary:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of
items.text:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".
  - Published27 November 2020
